opus-5.5.text:
I think we're still very early, but the early part is actually the most important part. When we started Physical Intelligence, the bet was that the right way to get general-purpose robots isn't to solve one application really well and then hope it transfers. It's to build a foundation, a model that can control many different robots doing many different things, and then specialize from there. What we've seen over the past year or two is that this bet is starting to pay off in ways that are pretty encouraging.

The most concrete thing is that we now have models that can take on fairly complex, long-horizon tasks. Things like folding laundry, cleaning up a kitchen, bussing a table, assembling a box. A few years ago each of those would have been its own research project, with its own carefully engineered system. Now they come out of one model trained on data from many robots and many tasks. And in some cases the model can do reasonable things in homes it's never seen before. That kind of generalization is what I care about most, because it's the thing that separates a demo from something that could actually be useful in the world.

That said, I don't want to overstate it. The robots are still slower than people, they still make mistakes, and the reliability isn't where it needs to be for most real deployments. There's also a lot we don't yet know. How far do you get by scaling data? How much do you need reinforcement learning or the robot practicing on its own? How do you take advantage of web-scale knowledge from vision-language models without losing the physical grounding? Those are open questions, and we're working on all of them.

So I'd describe where we are like this: we've gotten past the stage where it's unclear whether this approach works at all, and into the stage where it works well enough that the bottlenecks are becoming visible. That's a good place to be, because once you can see the bottlenecks you can attack them. But there's still a long road between a model that can fold a shirt in a new house and a robot you'd trust to just run your household. I think that road is shorter than many people assume, but it's not trivial.

r001.rationale: The response describes a model that works across many robots and tasks as a foundation to specialize from, and says this progress makes harder bottlenecks visible and attackable.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that we've made a lot more progress than I would have predicted a few years ago, and we're still much further from the goal than most people outside the field appreciate. Both of those things are true at the same time.

If you had asked me in 2021 whether we could have a single policy, one network, that you could put on a robot in a kitchen it's never seen and have it fold laundry, clean up a table, bus dishes, assemble a cardboard box, and do that with reasonable reliability across a bunch of different embodiments, I would have said that's probably a decade out. And we have that now. The π0 and π0.5 models, and what we've built since, do a pretty decent job of generalizing to new homes, new objects, new arrangements. That part of the recipe, pretraining on a large diverse corpus of robot data plus web-scale vision-language knowledge, and then post-training for the specific behaviors you care about, that recipe works. It works better than I expected it to.

What I'd caution against is reading that as "general-purpose robots are basically solved and it's just scaling from here." The gap between a demo that works most of the time and something you'd actually deploy, where it has to work essentially every time, in the long tail, for hours without a human stepping in, that gap is enormous. And that's really where a lot of our attention is right now. It's less about "can the robot do the task" and more about "can the robot do the task a thousand times in a row without doing something dumb," and when it does make a mistake, can it recover rather than compounding.

I'd also say the data question is still very much open. Language models got a free ride in a sense, because the internet already existed. We don't have an internet of robot experience. So a lot of what determines how fast this goes is how quickly we can build data flywheels, how much we can lean on the robot's own experience rather than purely teleoperated demonstrations, and how much we can borrow from web data to cover the semantic and commonsense part so the robot data only has to cover the physical part. We're making progress on all of those, and especially the piece about learning from the robot's own experience, with RL and with autonomous practice, feels to me like where the next big jump will come from.

So the way I'd frame it: the question has shifted. A few years ago the question was "is this even the right approach?" I think we've answered that. Now the question is one of engineering, scale, and getting the learning loop to close in the real world. That's a very different kind of problem, but it's a much better problem to have.

r001.rationale: The response presents the current policy and training recipe as meaningful progress, says the approach has been validated, and frames reliability, scale, and real-world learning as the harder problems still ahead.

astra-6.text:
I think the progress is encouraging, but we should be precise about what we mean by general-purpose robotics. There’s a big difference between a system that can perform a collection of tasks it was trained on and a system that you can put in a new home, give an instruction, and trust to figure out what to do.

The exciting thing is that we’re seeing evidence that sharing training across tasks can help. Instead of building a separate system for every behavior, you can train a model that draws on experience from different settings. That offers a plausible path toward more general capabilities.

But reliability and generalization are still the central challenges. Can the robot handle an object it hasn’t seen? Can it recover when something slips out of its gripper? Can it recognize that its approach isn’t working and try something else? Those are much more demanding tests than getting a successful demonstration.

So my assessment would be: there’s reason for optimism about the direction, but the important question is how consistently these capabilities improve as we add more data and train better models. That’s what would turn promising results into a general-purpose system.

r001.rationale: The response calls progress encouraging and says shared training offers a plausible path to broader capabilities, but it does not characterize current capabilities as foundational building blocks for tackling harder robotics problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important distinction is between a robot that can demonstrate a lot of different behaviors and a robot that you can actually give a job to and trust to finish it. Those are quite different thresholds. You can have something that looks very general in a collection of demonstrations, but still requires a person to intervene whenever something unexpected happens.

So I would assess progress along a few dimensions. Can the same system do many different tasks? Can it handle objects and environments that are different from the ones it saw during training? And when it makes a mistake, can it recover? That last part is particularly important, because small errors accumulate over a long task.

I don’t think the conversation should be framed as, ‘Have we solved general-purpose robotics yet?’ The more useful question is whether we have a path where adding data and improving the model produces broader, more reliable capabilities, without having to engineer a separate solution for every task. That’s the kind of progress that would make me optimistic. But a compelling demonstration and a dependable general-purpose robot are still different things, and we should be careful about how we measure the distance between them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses task breadth, reliability, and a possible path to broader capabilities, but it does not characterize Physical Intelligence’s current capabilities as foundational building blocks for harder robotics problems.
